title: Quantum Mechanics — Wave-Particle Duality & the Quantum World

subChunks.title: Quantum Mechanics — Wave-Particle Duality & the Quantum World

storyBeats.txt: Theodora dimmed the lantern until only a pale glow remained. "Classical physics," she said, "gives you a universe of definite positions, definite speeds, and perfectly predictable outcomes. It is a beautiful clockwork. And it is wrong — at small scales."

"In 1900, Max Planck saved physics from an embarrassing infinity by proposing that energy comes in discrete packets — quanta. He didn't entirely believe it himself. Five years later, Einstein used the same idea to explain why shining light on metal ejects electrons in a way no wave theory could account for. The quantum revolution had begun, and nobody would emerge from it with their intuitions intact."

"What followed was twenty years of the most intense intellectual work in the history of science — Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Dirac, Born, Pauli. At the end of it, they had a theory of stunning accuracy that none of them could quite agree on how to interpret. That situation has not entirely changed."

"Quantum mechanics is not just an abstract puzzle. It explains the periodic table, chemical bonding, lasers, transistors, MRI scanners, and the fact that you do not fall through your chair. The floor beneath you is solid because electrons obey the Pauli Exclusion Principle. Quantum weirdness is the reason ordinary matter behaves the way it does."

subChunks.hookHtml: Quantum mechanics is the theory governing the behaviour of matter and energy at atomic and subatomic scales. It replaced classical physics in the early 20th century after a series of experiments — blackbody radiation, the photoelectric effect, atomic emission spectra — that classical theory simply could not explain. The resulting framework is mathematically precise, experimentally impeccable, and conceptually strange: particles behave as waves, measurements disturb the systems they observe, and nature has fundamental limits on what can be simultaneously known.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Quantum Revolution — Historical Background

Blackbody radiation (Planck, 1900): Classical theory predicted that a hot object should radiate infinite energy at short wavelengths (the "ultraviolet catastrophe"). Planck resolved this by assuming energy is emitted in discrete quanta: E = hf, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s (Planck's constant) and f is frequency. This was the birth of quantum theory.

Photoelectric effect (Einstein, 1905): Light shining on a metal surface ejects electrons — but only if the frequency exceeds a threshold, regardless of intensity. Einstein explained this by treating light as packets of energy (photons): E = hf. Below the threshold frequency, no single photon has enough energy to eject an electron; increasing intensity only increases the number of photons, not their individual energy. This won Einstein the Nobel Prize in 1921.

Atomic spectra (Bohr model, 1913): Hydrogen emits light only at specific wavelengths (emission spectrum). Bohr proposed electrons occupy discrete energy levels; photon emission/absorption occurs when electrons jump between levels: ΔE = hf. The Bohr model correctly predicted hydrogen's spectrum but failed for multi-electron atoms.

Wave-Particle Duality

de Broglie wavelength (1924): If light (a wave) can behave as particles, perhaps particles have wave properties? de Broglie proposed: λ = h/p = h/mv. For an electron moving at 1% of c: λ ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ m — the scale of atomic spacing, explaining electron diffraction. For a tennis ball (0.06 kg at 30 m/s): λ ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³⁴ m — completely undetectable. Quantum effects only matter at small scales.

Double-slit experiment: When electrons (or photons) are fired one at a time through two slits, an interference pattern builds up on the detector — as if each electron passes through both slits simultaneously as a wave. But when a detector is placed to observe which slit the electron passes through, the interference pattern vanishes and electrons behave like particles. Observation collapses the wave-like behaviour. This is one of the most disturbing results in all of physics.

The Uncertainty Principle

Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle (1927): It is impossible to simultaneously know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a particle: Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2, where ℏ = h/2π = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. This is NOT a statement about measurement technology — it is a fundamental property of nature. Similarly: ΔE · Δt ≥ ℏ/2 (energy-time uncertainty).

Consequence: electrons in an atom cannot be stationary — a precisely known momentum of zero would require infinite positional uncertainty, but the electron must be somewhere near the nucleus. The resulting ground-state energy prevents electrons from collapsing into the nucleus.

Wave Functions and Probability

Schrödinger's wave equation (1926): Describes how quantum states evolve over time. The wave function ψ (psi) encodes all information about a quantum system. The probability of finding a particle at position x is |ψ(x)|² — the square of the wave function's amplitude. Before measurement, the particle exists in a superposition of all possible states.

Copenhagen Interpretation (Bohr/Heisenberg): The wave function is not a physical wave but a probability amplitude. Upon measurement, it "collapses" to a definite value. Between measurements, quantum systems exist in superposition. Other interpretations (Many-Worlds, Pilot Wave) exist but remain philosophically contested.

Schrödinger's Cat: A thought experiment illustrating the measurement problem — a cat in a box is both alive and dead (superposition) until the box is opened. At macroscopic scales, decoherence (interaction with the environment) destroys quantum superpositions almost instantly, explaining why everyday objects behave classically.

Quantum Numbers and Atomic Structure

In the full quantum mechanical model, electrons in atoms are described by four quantum numbers:

  • Principal quantum number (n): 1, 2, 3... — energy level/shell
  • Angular momentum quantum number (l): 0 to n−1 — subshell shape (s, p, d, f)
  • Magnetic quantum number (mₗ): −l to +l — orbital orientation
  • Spin quantum number (mₛ): +½ or −½ — electron spin (up or down)

Pauli Exclusion Principle: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers. This limits each orbital to two electrons (spin up + spin down) and is the reason the periodic table has the structure it does — and the reason matter is solid.

Applications of Quantum Mechanics

Lasers: Stimulated emission (Einstein, 1917) — a photon triggers an excited atom to emit an identical photon (same phase, wavelength, direction) → coherent light.

Transistors and semiconductors: Band theory (quantum mechanical allowed energy bands) explains conductors, insulators, and semiconductors. The entire electronics industry depends on quantum mechanics.

MRI scanners: Exploit nuclear magnetic resonance — quantum mechanical spin of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field.

Quantum tunnelling: Particles can cross energy barriers they classically could not — basis of nuclear fusion in stars, radioactive alpha decay, tunnel diodes, and scanning tunnelling microscopes.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what the double-slit experiment reveals about the nature of electrons — why it is so strange, and what it tells us about quantum reality.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A photoelectric effect experiment uses ultraviolet light on a sodium surface. The work function of sodium (the minimum energy needed to eject an electron) is 3.65 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. (1) Calculate the threshold frequency below which no electrons are ejected. (2) Light of frequency 1.2 × 10¹⁵ Hz illuminates the surface. Calculate the energy of a single photon. (3) Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron. (4) A student doubles the intensity of the light while keeping frequency constant. Explain what changes and what stays the same in terms of the ejected electrons.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) At threshold, photon energy = work function: hf₀ = Φ. f₀ = Φ/h = (3.65 × 10⁻¹⁹) / (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴) = 5.51 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Below this frequency, no electrons are ejected regardless of intensity.

(2) E = hf = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.2 × 10¹⁵ = 7.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

(3) Maximum KE = E − Φ = 7.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 3.65 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. This is the Einstein photoelectric equation: KE_max = hf − Φ.

(4) Doubling intensity doubles the number of photons per second — so twice as many electrons are ejected per second (the photocurrent doubles). However, the maximum kinetic energy of each electron is unchanged because it depends only on the frequency (energy per photon), not intensity. Each photon still has the same energy; more photons means more electrons, not faster ones. This was the key insight that classical wave theory could not explain: intensity should increase electron energy if light were purely a wave, but it does not.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: An electron is confined in a box of width 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (roughly the size of an atom). (1) Using the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle (Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2), estimate the minimum uncertainty in the electron's momentum if its position uncertainty is the width of the box. (2) Use this momentum to estimate the minimum kinetic energy of the electron (KE = p²/2m, where m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg). Express your answer in electron-volts (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). (3) A tennis ball (mass 60 g) is "confined" in a box of width 1.0 m. Estimate the minimum kinetic energy from the same principle. (4) Why does the uncertainty principle have no observable consequences for the tennis ball but enormous consequences for the electron? What does this tell us about why quantum effects are only apparent at small scales?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Δx = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Δp ≥ ℏ/(2Δx) = (1.055 × 10⁻³⁴) / (2 × 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 5.28 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s.

(2) KE = p²/2m = (5.28 × 10⁻²⁵)² / (2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 2.79 × 10⁻⁴⁹ / 1.82 × 10⁻³⁰ = 1.53 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. In eV: 1.53 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 0.96 eV. This is comparable to atomic binding energies — the uncertainty principle literally sets the energy scale of chemistry.

(3) Tennis ball: Δp ≥ ℏ/(2Δx) = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ / 2.0 = 5.28 × 10⁻³⁵ kg·m/s. KE = p²/2m = (5.28 × 10⁻³⁵)² / (2 × 0.06) = 2.32 × 10⁻⁶⁸ J. This is astronomically small — 10⁴⁹ times smaller than any energy we could detect. The tennis ball's quantum zero-point energy is completely negligible compared to any macroscopic energy scale.

(4) The ratio of quantum zero-point energy to the object's typical mechanical energy scales as ℏ/(mL·v). For an electron: m ≈ 10⁻³⁰ kg, L ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m — the resulting energy (≈1 eV) is comparable to thermal and chemical energies, so quantum effects dominate. For a macroscopic object: m ≈ 10⁻¹ kg, L ≈ 1 m — the quantum energy (≈10⁻⁶⁸ J) is completely undetectable against thermal fluctuations of ≈10⁻²¹ J. Quantum mechanics is not a different kind of physics from classical — it is the same physics, but at human scales ℏ is so small relative to the relevant energies that quantum effects are entirely invisible. The boundary is not sharp; it is set by the ratio ℏ/(action of the system).
learningObjectives: Explain the photoelectric effect using Einstein's photon model and calculate photon energies and maximum electron kinetic energies.
Describe wave-particle duality, de Broglie wavelength, and what the double-slit experiment reveals about quantum measurement.
State Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and apply it to estimate minimum momentum and energy for confined particles.
Explain how quantum numbers, the Pauli Exclusion Principle, and wave functions underpin atomic structure and the periodic table.
commonMistakes: Thinking the uncertainty principle is about measurement precision — it is not a technological limitation but a fundamental property of nature; even a perfect measurement cannot simultaneously fix both position and momentum.
Confusing photon energy with intensity — energy per photon depends on frequency (E=hf); intensity affects how many photons arrive, not the energy of each individual photon.

Believing the double-slit interference pattern is due to photons or electrons interacting with each other — the pattern appears even when particles are sent one at a time, showing each single particle interferes with itself.

Treating Schrödinger's cat as a statement about macroscopic superposition — in practice, decoherence destroys quantum superpositions at macroscopic scales almost instantaneously; the thought experiment illustrates the measurement problem, not a prediction that cats are literally in superpositions.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly applies E=hf and the photoelectric equation (KE_max = hf − Φ) to calculate photon energies, threshold frequencies, and electron kinetic energies.
Accurately explains wave-particle duality and the role of observation in the double-slit experiment without misrepresenting the underlying physics.
Applies the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle quantitatively and explains why quantum effects are unobservable at macroscopic scales.
Describes quantum numbers, the Pauli Exclusion Principle, and at least two real-world applications of quantum mechanics (e.g. lasers, transistors, tunnelling).

rabbitHoleTerms.description: When two particles interact, their quantum states can become correlated regardless of separation distance — measuring one instantly determines the state of the other. Einstein called this "spooky action at a distance" and doubted it was real; Bell's theorem (1964) and subsequent experiments confirmed it is genuine. It is the basis of quantum cryptography and quantum computing.

A quantum particle can pass through an energy barrier it classically could not surmount — because the wave function has a non-zero amplitude on the far side. This drives nuclear fusion in stars (protons tunnel through the Coulomb barrier at temperatures much lower than classically required), radioactive alpha decay, and scanning tunnelling microscopes.

The fundamental equation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics: iℏ ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ. It describes how the wave function ψ evolves over time under a Hamiltonian operator Ĥ. For bound states (like electrons in atoms), it produces discrete energy levels — directly explaining atomic spectra.

The process by which a quantum superposition is destroyed through interaction with the environment. Environmental particles "measure" the quantum system, causing it to effectively collapse into a definite state. Decoherence explains why everyday objects behave classically despite being composed of quantum particles, and is the central challenge in building quantum computers.

A 1964 mathematical proof by John Bell showing that no local hidden-variable theory can reproduce all predictions of quantum mechanics. Experiments by Aspect (1982) and many subsequent groups have violated Bell inequalities, confirming that quantum mechanics is genuinely non-local — there are no hidden classical variables underlying quantum randomness.

questions.questionHtml: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz strikes a metal with work function 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
questions.explanationHtml: Photon energy: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 8.0 × 10¹⁴ = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Maximum KE = E − Φ = 5.30 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 2.50 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.80 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Since photon energy > work function, electrons are ejected. The maximum kinetic energy is the photon energy minus the minimum energy needed to escape the metal surface.

questions.questionHtml: An electron has de Broglie wavelength 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Which statement correctly describes what this means? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
options: The electron physically oscillates with a wavelength of 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m as it travels
The electron's momentum is p = h/λ = 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s, and it will undergo wave-like diffraction when passing through a gap of comparable size
The electron can only exist at positions separated by multiples of 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m
questions.correctAnswer: The electron's momentum is p = h/λ = 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s, and it will undergo wave-like diffraction when passing through a gap of comparable size
questions.explanationHtml: The de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p gives the wavelength of the probability wave associated with the particle. It does not mean the electron physically oscillates — the wave is a probability amplitude (wave function). A particle with this wavelength will undergo diffraction and interference when it encounters apertures or obstacles of comparable size (≈10⁻¹⁰ m = atomic spacing). This is why electron diffraction by crystals is used to study crystal structure. The momentum: p = h/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s.

questions.questionHtml: A student argues: "The double-slit interference pattern proves that each electron splits in two and passes through both slits simultaneously as a physical object." Evaluate this claim.
options: Correct — the interference pattern can only arise if the electron physically divides and takes both paths

Incorrect — the electron does not split; rather, its wave function (probability amplitude) evolves through both slits and interferes, but when detected it always appears as a whole, indivisible particle at one location
Incorrect — the interference is caused by electrons interacting with each other as they pass through the two slits
Correct — but only at very low intensities; at high intensities electrons behave as classical particles
questions.correctAnswer: Incorrect — the electron does not split; rather, its wave function (probability amplitude) evolves through both slits and interferes, but when detected it always appears as a whole, indivisible particle at one location
questions.explanationHtml: The student's claim involves a common misinterpretation. Electrons are never detected as fragments — a detector always registers a whole electron at a single location. What undergoes interference is the wave function ψ, which describes the probability amplitude for finding the electron. The two paths through the slits produce components of ψ that interfere constructively and destructively at different positions on the screen. This interference pattern builds up dot by dot, even when electrons are sent one at a time — ruling out electron-electron interaction as the cause. The correct statement: the electron's probability amplitude passes through both slits and interferes; the electron itself is detected as a whole particle. This is the measurement problem at the heart of quantum mechanics — the transition from wave-like propagation to definite detection is what collapses the wave function.
